baits.hook: Tie the squarebill straight to your 12–15 lb line; it has its own hooks, so add no bait.

baits.name: Popper
baits.description: A floating fly with a flat or rounded head that pops and splashes on the water like a frog or bug that fell in.
baits.why: Bass eat frogs, mice and bugs that fall in the water, so a popper's pop and splash looks like one; shallow bass come up for it at dawn and dusk. AZGFD says the post-spawn topwater bite is hot early and late.
baits.hook: Tie the popper to the end of your leader; it comes already tied on its own hook.

gear.name: Rainbow trout
gear.where: Near the shore when the water is cool, and in deeper water once it warms.

methods.name: Bottom
methods.summary: Let bait rest on the bottom with a sinker and wait for a bite.
bring: Sliding sinker (a weight with a hole for your line)
Small swivel (a metal link that stops the sinker)
18 in leader (a short piece of line)
steps: Slide the sinker onto your line, then tie on a small swivel (a metal link that stops the sinker).
Tie an 18 in leader (a short piece of line) to the other end of the swivel.
Tie the hook to the end of the leader.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast out and let the sinker settle on the bottom.
methods.bite: Trout bite lightly. When the line pulls or the rod tip bends, lift the rod with a gentle pull and reel in.

methods.name: Spinner
methods.summary: Cast a small lure with a spinning blade and reel it back.
steps: Tie the spinner to the end of your line.
Cast it out.
Reel it back slowly and steadily, and try a different speed on the next cast.
methods.bite: If you feel a tug, lift the rod and keep reeling.

methods.name: Fly
methods.summary: Cast a fly that looks like a small fish or creature and pull it back by hand.
steps: Tie the woolly bugger to the end of your line.
Cast it out.
Pull the line back in slowly by hand.
methods.bite: If you feel a pull or the line stops, lift the rod and pull the line tight.

baits.name: PowerBait
baits.description: Soft, scented, brightly colored dough you mold onto the hook; it is made to look and smell like the feed pellets hatchery trout grew up on.
baits.why: Hatchery trout grew up eating feed pellets, so scented, colored dough that smells and looks like a pellet works best in the first days after a stocking. AZGFD lists PowerBait among its top trout baits.
baits.hook: Press a small ball of PowerBait around the size 10–12 hook until no metal shows. Bring two or three colors, like rainbow or chartreuse.

baits.name: Nightcrawler
baits.description: A big earthworm from a bait shop; you use a piece or the whole worm.
baits.why: Trout pick worms and bugs off the bottom, so a nightcrawler piece resting there looks like food they know. AZGFD lists worms first among its best trout baits all year; they work well in cold water, when trout cruise the shore.
baits.hook: Thread a small piece of nightcrawler onto the size 10–12 hook, leaving a short tail to wiggle.

baits.name: Corn
baits.description: Canned sweet corn, a pantry bait you put on the hook one or two kernels at a time.
baits.why: Stocked rainbows grew up on feed pellets, so a bright, sweet-smelling kernel of corn on the bottom is easy to mistake for food. AZGFD names corn with worms and PowerBait as its best-bet trout baits.
baits.hook: Push one or two kernels of canned corn onto the size 10–12 hook so the point is covered.

baits.name: Inline spinner
baits.description: A small metal lure with a spinning blade that flashes and thumps as you reel it in.
baits.why: Trout eat small fish and bugs near shore in cool water, so a small spinner's flash and thump looks like one swimming off. AZGFD says to think small for trout, in silver, gold or copper.
baits.hook: Tie the 1/16–1/8 oz inline spinner, like a Panther Martin, straight to your line; it has its own hook, so add no bait.

baits.name: Woolly bugger
baits.description: A fuzzy fly with a long tail that looks like a leech or a small fish when pulled slowly.
baits.why: Trout eat leeches and small fish, so a woolly bugger pulled slowly near shore or along pool bottoms looks like one. AZGFD lists size 10 bead-headed Woolly Buggers as producing flies for stocked trout all winter.
baits.hook: Tie a size 10 woolly bugger to the end of your leader; it comes already tied on its own hook.

photo.title: Black Woolly Bugger by Mike Cline
photo.author: Mike Cline

gear.name: Walleye
gear.where: Along rocky shores, especially rock that sticks out into the water.

methods.name: Jig
methods.summary: Put a worm or leech on a weighted hook and drag it slowly along the bottom.
bring: 1/4–3/8 oz jig head (a hook with a weighted head)
steps: Fish in low light or at night.
Tie the jig head to the end of your line.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast it out.
Reel it back slowly, lifting and lowering the rod tip so the jig hops along the bottom.
methods.bite: If the line twitches, jumps or goes slack, lift the rod and reel in.

methods.name: Bottom bouncer
methods.summary: Drag a nightcrawler on a hook line behind a weight that bumps along the bottom, from a slowly moving boat.
bring: Bottom bouncer (a lead weight on a stiff wire arm that bumps along the bottom)
Crawler harness (a spinning blade and two hooks on a short line, made for nightcrawlers)
steps: Fish in low light or at night.
Tie the bottom bouncer to the end of your line.
Tie the crawler harness behind it, so it trails 2 to 3 feet back.
Put your bait on the hook.
Let the weight touch the bottom, then slowly drag it along a rocky shore.
methods.bite: If the line twitches or moves off, lift the rod and reel in.

methods.name: Fly
methods.summary: Cast a fly that looks like a small fish or creature and pull it back by hand.
steps: Fish in low light or at night.
Tie the Clouser to the end of your line.
Cast it out.
Let it sink.
Pull it back in short pulls.
methods.bite: If you feel a pull or the line stops, lift the rod and pull the line tight.

baits.name: Nightcrawler
baits.description: A big earthworm from a bait shop; you use a piece or the whole worm.
baits.why: Walleye eat fish, insects and crayfish, mostly in low light, so a crawler wriggling on the bottom looks like an easy meal. AZGFD says nightcrawlers are a good bet for walleye; Iowa DNR advises crawlers in summer.
baits.hook: On the jig, thread the crawler on the hook (half a crawler is fine); on the harness, front on one hook, back on the other.

baits.name: Leech
baits.description: A live leech (a soft, wriggly pond worm), sold at bait shops.
baits.why: Walleye eat fish, insects and crayfish, mostly in low light, so a leech wriggling off a jig looks like an easy meal on the bottom. Iowa DNR advises leeches or crawlers in late spring, summer and early fall.
baits.hook: Hook the leech once through the sucker disk (its flat end) so it wiggles on the jig head.

baits.name: Clouser minnow
baits.description: A fly with lead eyes that dips and rises like a small baitfish when you pull the line in short tugs.
baits.why: Walleye eat mostly fish and feed in low light, so a Clouser, a weighted fly pulled in short tugs, dips like a baitfish; in dark colors it can pass for a leech. Fish it at night or at dawn.
baits.hook: Tie the size 4 Clouser to your leader; it has its own hook, so add no bait.

photo.title: A Fire Tiger Clouser minnow fly
photo.author: Mike Cline

gear.name: Yellow bass
gear.where: In schools, just off the bottom.

methods.name: Bobber
methods.summary: Hang bait under a bobber and wait for the bobber to dip.
steps: Tie the hook to the end of your line.
Clip the bobber onto the line so the bait hangs just above the bottom.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast it out.
methods.bite: When the bobber goes under, lift the rod and reel in.

methods.name: Jig
methods.summary: Cast a small weighted hook with a bit of worm and bounce it just off the bottom.
bring: 1/16 oz white or chartreuse jig (a hook with a weighted head)
steps: Tie the jig to the end of your line.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast near a school of fish.
Let it sink to the bottom.
Lift and drop it, keeping it within a few inches of the bottom.
methods.bite: If the line twitches or moves off, lift the rod and reel in.

methods.name: Fly
methods.summary: Cast a fly that looks like a small fish or creature and pull it back by hand.
steps: Tie the fly to the end of your line.
Cast it near a school of fish.
Pull it back in short pulls.
methods.bite: If you feel a pull or the line stops, lift the rod and pull the line tight.

baits.name: Nightcrawler
baits.description: A big earthworm from a bait shop; you use a piece or the whole worm.
baits.why: Yellow bass feed heavily on small creatures on the bottom, so a small piece of nightcrawler is real food. AZGFD names small nightcrawler pieces for yellow bass; Iowa DNR says a piece about an inch long is plenty.
baits.hook: Thread a 1 in piece of nightcrawler onto the size 8 hook (or the jig) so it covers the point.

baits.name: Streamer
baits.description: A fly that imitates a minnow or other small fish, from a small marabou one to a big sculpin pattern, pulled back in short strips.
baits.why: Yellow bass eat small fish and bottom insects, so a small white streamer pulled in short tugs and kept low looks like a minnow on the move.
baits.hook: Tie the size 8 streamer to your leader; it has its own hook, so add no bait.

baits.name: Clouser minnow
baits.description: A fly with lead eyes that dips and rises like a small baitfish when you pull the line in short tugs.
baits.why: Adult yellow bass eat fish and school near the surface, so a Clouser, a weighted fly pulled in short tugs, dips like a small baitfish. It is a proven fly for white bass, a close relative.
baits.hook: Tie the size 8 Clouser to your leader; it has its own hook, so add no bait.

photo.title: A Fire Tiger Clouser minnow fly
photo.author: Mike Cline

gear.name: Channel catfish
gear.where: On the bottom: in the deepest spots by day, and in shallower water after dark.

methods.name: Bottom
methods.summary: Let bait rest on the bottom with a sinker and wait for a bite.
bring: Size 2–4 circle hook (a round hook that sets itself)
1/2 oz sliding sinker (a weight with a hole; your line slides through it)
Swivel (a small metal link that stops the sinker)
12–18 in leader (a short piece of line)
steps: Slide the sinker onto your line, then tie the swivel to the end.
Tie the hook to the leader, then tie the other end of the leader to the swivel.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast out and let it settle on the bottom.
methods.bite: When the rod tip bends down and stays down, pick up the rod and reel in steadily. Do not jerk the rod: the circle hook sets itself.

methods.name: Cut bait
methods.summary: Put a chunk of fresh fish on the bottom where catfish feed at dusk.
bring: Size 2–4 circle hook (a round hook that sets itself)
1/2 oz sliding sinker (a weight with a hole; your line slides through it)
Swivel (a small metal link that stops the sinker)
12–18 in leader (a short piece of line)
steps: Go at dusk.
Slide the sinker onto your line, then tie the swivel to the end.
Tie the hook to the leader, then tie the other end of the leader to the swivel.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast off the deep side of a point (land sticking out into the water) and let it settle on the bottom.
methods.bite: When the rod tip bends down and stays down, pick up the rod and reel in steadily. Do not jerk the rod: the circle hook sets itself.

baits.name: Hot dog
baits.description: A plain hot dog cut into chunks, a cheap store-bought bait.
baits.why: Catfish hunt by smell, not sight, so the stronger a bait smells, the better: a cut hot dog leaks salty, fatty scent they follow along the bottom. Fish it deep in daytime and shallower after dark.
baits.hook: Cut the hot dog into bite-size chunks and thread one onto the size 2–4 circle hook, point out.

baits.name: Chicken liver
baits.description: Raw chicken liver from the grocery store, a soft and smelly bait.
baits.why: Catfish find food by smell, taste and touch, so raw liver that bleeds a strong scent of blood and meat along the bottom pulls them in from far off; the stronger and ranker, the better. Best at dusk and after dark.
baits.hook: Thread a piece of liver onto the size 2–4 circle hook two or three times so it stays on through the cast.

photo.title: Raw chicken livers on a cutting board
photo.author: Poupou l'quourouce

baits.name: Stink bait
baits.description: A smelly store-bought paste or dip bait sold in a tub.
baits.why: Catfish find food mostly by smell and taste, so the more rancid the better: stink bait is made to smell rotten, and the stench spreads far through the water. AZGFD reports name stink baits, dips and nuggets.
baits.hook: Press the store-bought stink bait onto a plastic worm or sponge on the size 2–4 hook so it does not wash off.

baits.name: Cut bait
baits.description: A chunk of fresh fish (shad, carp or bluegill) cut to fit the hook.
baits.why: Channel cats eat fish, insects and crayfish and feed at night, so a fresh chunk of shad, carp or bluegill on the bottom at dusk looks and smells like an easy meal. Use only those: other game fish can't be cut for bait in Arizona.
baits.hook: Cut a fresh fish into a chunk that covers the size 2–4 circle hook, and run the hook through the skin once with the point out.

gear.name: Common carp
gear.where: In shallow water.

methods.name: Bottom
methods.summary: Let corn or dough bait sit on the bottom and wait for a bite.
steps: Tie the hook to the end of your line.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast it out and let it sink to the bottom.
Rest the rod and watch the line. Carp can take a while.
methods.bite: When the line pulls tight or the rod bends, lift the rod and hold on. Carp run hard, so let line slip off the reel.

methods.name: Fly
methods.summary: Cast a small fly to a carp you can see in shallow water.
steps: Look for carp in shallow water.
Tie the fly to the end of your line.
Cast the fly near a carp you can see.
Let it sink.
methods.bite: If you feel a pull or the line stops, lift the rod and pull the line tight.

baits.name: Corn
baits.description: Canned sweet corn, a pantry bait you put on the hook one or two kernels at a time.
baits.why: Corn isn't wild carp food, but carp feed mostly from the bottom and find food more by taste than sight, so sweet corn draws them. AZGFD recommends corn on a slip sinker rig in Phoenix-area ponds and lakes in the warm months.
baits.hook: Thread two or three kernels of canned corn onto the size 6 hook, covering the point.

baits.name: Dough bait
baits.description: A soft, sweet-smelling paste of flour or bread that you mold onto the hook.
baits.why: Carp feed on the bottom and find food more by taste than sight, so a sweet, flavored dough ball fished there draws them. Dough balls are one of the most common carp baits; wait, because carp can take a while.
baits.hook: Mold a marble-size ball of dough bait around the size 6 hook so the hook is covered.

baits.name: Nymph
baits.description: A small sinking fly that looks like an insect larva.
baits.why: Carp eat aquatic insects and other food off the bottom, so a nymph or crayfish fly looks like a meal. AZGFD says to cast 5–10 feet ahead of a carp you can see; carp craws worked in muddy water.
baits.hook: Tie the size 8 crayfish or carp nymph to the end of your line, cast 5–10 feet ahead of a carp you can see, and let it sink.

gear.name: Crappie
gear.where: Around brush and docks.

methods.name: Float
methods.summary: Hang a small jig under a float and wait for the float to dip.
bring: Small float (a bobber that clips onto the line)
steps: Go in early spring or fall, when they bite best.
Tie the jig to the end of your line.
Clip the float onto the line above the jig, so the jig hangs at least a foot off the bottom.
Cast near brush or a dock.
methods.bite: When the float goes under, lift the rod gently and reel in. Do not yank: crappie have soft mouths.

methods.name: Slip float
methods.summary: Hang a jig under a float that slides, so you can set how deep the jig hangs.
bring: Float stopper (a small knot or bead on your line that stops the float at the depth you pick)
Slip float (a bobber with a hole through it that slides along the line)
steps: Put the float stopper on your line, a few feet from the end.
Slide the slip float onto your line below the stopper.
Tie the jig to the end of your line.
Slide the stopper up or down to set how deep the jig hangs, at least a foot off the bottom. If you get no bites, try another depth.
Cast near brush or a dock. The jig sinks until the stopper reaches the float.
methods.bite: When the float goes under, lift the rod gently and reel in. Do not yank: crappie have soft mouths.

methods.name: Fly
methods.summary: Cast a fly that looks like a small fish or creature and pull it back by hand.
steps: Tie the streamer to the end of your line.
Cast it near brush or a dock.
Pull it back in short pulls.
methods.bite: If you feel a pull or the line stops, lift the rod and pull the line tight.

baits.name: Marabou jig
baits.description: A small weighted hook with a soft feather tail that flutters like a minnow or bug.
baits.why: Crappie eat minnows, young shad and insects, so a feathery 1/32 oz jig that flutters like one works. A float keeps it at one depth in front of brush, where crappie hold and bite slowly.
baits.hook: Tie the 1/32 oz marabou jig straight to your line, add no bait, and clip the float above it so the jig hangs at least a foot off the bottom.

baits.name: Tube jig
baits.description: A weighted hook with a hollow soft plastic body (the tube) that flutters as it sinks.
baits.why: Crappie eat small shad and bugs, so a hollow tube body fluttering on the fall looks like one. ODWC lists naturally colored tubes among the best crappie lures.
baits.hook: Tie the 1/32 oz tube jig straight to your line with the tube already on the weighted head and the hook point out, and set the float above it.

baits.name: Curly-tail grub
baits.description: A soft plastic body with a curling tail that wiggles as it sinks, threaded onto a small jig head.
baits.why: Crappie eat small shad, minnows and bugs, so a curly-tail grub wiggling as it sinks looks like one. AZGFD reports crappie biting 2-inch grubs bounced off the bottom, and Oklahoma lists curly-tail grubs.
baits.hook: Tie the 1.5 in curly-tail jig straight to your line, tail already on the weighted head; the slip float sets how deep it hangs.

baits.name: Streamer
baits.description: A fly that imitates a minnow or other small fish, from a small marabou one to a big sculpin pattern, pulled back in short strips.
baits.why: Minnows and young shad are what black crappie eat most, so a marabou streamer that pulses like a small minnow looks like a meal. Pull it back in short pulls along brush or weeds.
baits.hook: Tie the size 10 marabou streamer to the end of your leader; it comes already tied on its own hook.

gear.name: Flathead catfish
gear.where: On the bottom, near sunken trees and in deep holes where big fish hide.

methods.name: Bottom
methods.summary: Let bait rest on the bottom with a sinker and wait for a bite.
bring: 2/0–6/0 circle hook (a round hook that sets itself)
1–4 oz sliding sinker (a weight with a hole; your line slides through it)
Swivel (a small metal link that stops the sinker)
12–20 in leader of 25–30 lb line (a short piece of line)
steps: Go at night, or at dusk.
Slide the sinker onto your line, then tie the swivel to the end.
Tie the hook to the leader, then tie the other end of the leader to the swivel.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast near sunken trees or a deep hole and let it settle on the bottom.
methods.bite: When the rod tip bends down and stays down, pick up the rod and reel in steadily. Do not jerk the rod: the circle hook sets itself.

methods.name: Nightcrawlers
methods.summary: Put a big bunch of nightcrawlers on a large hook and let it rest on the bottom.
bring: 2/0–6/0 circle hook (a round hook that sets itself)
1–4 oz sliding sinker (a weight with a hole; your line slides through it)
Swivel (a small metal link that stops the sinker)
12–20 in leader of 25–30 lb line (a short piece of line)
steps: Go at night, or at dusk.
Slide the sinker onto your line, then tie the swivel to the end.
Tie the hook to the leader, then tie the other end of the leader to the swivel.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast near sunken trees or a deep hole and let it settle on the bottom.
methods.bite: When the rod tip bends down and stays down, pick up the rod and reel in steadily. Do not jerk the rod: the circle hook sets itself.

baits.name: Cut bait
baits.description: A chunk of fresh fish (shad, carp or bluegill) cut to fit the hook.
baits.why: Flatheads hunt live fish and crayfish at night and rarely eat old or rotting food, so a big chunk of fresh-cut shad, carp or bluegill, still bloody and smelly, works best near sunken trees or deep holes.
baits.hook: Push the 2/0–6/0 circle hook once through a big chunk of fresh fish, not stink bait, through the skin, with the point out.

baits.name: Nightcrawler
baits.description: A big earthworm from a bait shop; you use a piece or the whole worm.
baits.why: Flatheads feed at night in deep holes and heavy cover, so a big squirming bunch of worms gives off scent and motion they can find in the dark. Minnesota DNR says flatheads take gobs of crawlers, mostly at dusk and night.
baits.hook: Thread a big bunch of nightcrawlers onto the 2/0–6/0 circle hook until the hook is buried in a squirming ball.

gear.name: Largemouth bass
gear.where: Near reeds and docks.

methods.name: Plastic worm
methods.summary: Cast a soft plastic worm with no weight and let it sink slowly.
bring: Size 3/0 worm hook (a wide hook made for soft plastic worms)
steps: Tie the hook to the end of your line.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast it near reeds or docks.
Let it sink slowly on a loose line.
methods.bite: If the line twitches or moves off, lift the rod hard and reel in.

methods.name: Crankbait
methods.summary: Cast a hard plastic lure with a lip that makes it dive and wobble as you reel it back.
steps: Go at first light.
Tie the crankbait to the end of your line.
Cast it along rocks.
Reel it back.
methods.bite: If you feel a tug, lift the rod and keep reeling.

methods.name: Fly
methods.summary: Cast a floating bug and make it pop on the surface.
steps: Go at dawn.
Tie the popper to the end of your line.
Cast it near reeds or docks.
Pull the line in short tugs so it pops on the surface.
methods.bite: If a fish takes the fly, lift the rod.

baits.name: Senko
baits.description: A thick, soft plastic stick worm that wiggles as it sinks.
baits.why: Bass eat fish, crayfish and big insects, so a 5 in green-pumpkin Senko's slow, wiggling fall looks like an easy meal, especially on slow days or in shallow cover. AZGFD reports name Senkos at Lake Pleasant, Roosevelt and the Lower Salt.
baits.hook: Push the 3/0 worm hook through the tip of the Senko's head, bring it out, turn it, and tuck the hook point back into the worm so it won't snag weeds.

baits.name: Squarebill crankbait
baits.description: A hard plastic lure with a flat lip that makes it dive and wobble as you reel it in.
baits.why: Small fish and crayfish are a bass's main foods, so a lipped crankbait that wobbles and bumps along looks like one. AZGFD reports a good crankbait bite early in the day, and suggests it when topwater slows.
baits.hook: Tie the squarebill straight to your 12–15 lb line; it has its own hooks, so add no bait.

baits.name: Popper
baits.description: A floating fly with a flat or rounded head that pops and splashes on the water like a frog or bug that fell in.
baits.why: Bass eat frogs, mice and bugs that fall in the water, so a popper's pop and splash looks like one; shallow bass come up for it at dawn and dusk. AZGFD says the post-spawn topwater bite is hot early and late.
baits.hook: Tie the popper to the end of your leader; it comes already tied on its own hook.

gear.name: Smallmouth bass
gear.where: Along rocks, and on rocky ledges and rock that sticks out into the water.

methods.name: Jig
methods.summary: Cast a soft lure on a small weighted hook and work it along the rocks.
bring: 1/8 oz jig head (a hook with a weighted head)
steps: Tie the jig head to the end of your line.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast it near rocks.
Reel it back along the rocks.
methods.bite: If the line twitches or moves off, lift the rod and reel in.

methods.name: Drop shot
methods.summary: Tie a hook about a foot above a weight, so a soft bait hangs just off the bottom.
bring: Size 1 drop-shot hook (a small hook made for this rig)
1/4 oz drop-shot weight (a small teardrop weight that ties to the end of your line)
steps: Tie the hook to your line, leaving about a foot of line hanging below the knot.
Tie the weight to the end of that hanging line.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast to a rocky ledge or rocky shore, let the weight sit on the bottom, and gently shake the rod tip.
methods.bite: Watch your line, because bites can be very light. If it twitches or moves off, lift the rod and reel in.

methods.name: Fly
methods.summary: Cast a fly that looks like a small fish or creature and pull it back by hand.
steps: Tie the fly to the end of your line.
Cast it near rocks.
Let it sink.
Pull it back slowly by hand.
methods.bite: If you feel a pull or the line stops, lift the rod and pull the line tight.

baits.name: Crayfish soft plastic
baits.description: A soft rubber lure shaped like a crayfish, made to bump along the bottom.
baits.why: Smallmouth eat a lot of crayfish, so a crayfish soft plastic bumped along the rocks looks like one. AZGFD reports say small soft plastic crayfish and jigs work in fall, and plastics on rocky shelves in spring.
baits.hook: Push the point of the 1/8 oz jig head into the nose of the plastic and out along its back, so the body hangs straight.

baits.name: Tube jig
baits.description: A weighted hook with a hollow soft plastic body (the tube) that flutters as it sinks.
baits.why: Smallmouth eat crayfish and small fish, so a tube's hollow, wiggling tentacles dropping through the water look like one. AZGFD reports tube jigs catching smallmouth at Lake Mohave and on rocky ledges at Lake Powell.
baits.hook: Slide the tube over the 1/8 oz jig head until the line-tie pokes out the closed end, with the hook point just outside the tube.

baits.name: Plastic worm
baits.description: A soft rubber worm, thick or thin, that you put on a hook and let sink slowly.
baits.why: Smallmouth eat fish, crayfish and large insects, so a thin worm hanging just off the bottom looks like an easy meal when they ignore bigger baits. AZGFD names small drop-shot worms and light, subtle plastics in summer.
baits.hook: Push the size 1 drop-shot hook through the worm's nose once, point out, so it hangs straight and quivers when you shake the rod.

baits.name: Swimbait
baits.description: A soft plastic minnow with a paddle tail that wiggles as you reel it in.
baits.why: Smallmouth eat small fish like shad, so a swimbait, a soft plastic minnow, looks like one. AZGFD reports say swimbaits keep producing smallmouth, including around rock ledges in 10–30 feet of water in June.
baits.hook: Push the size 1 drop-shot hook through the nose of the 3 in minnow plastic, point out, so it hangs level in the water.

baits.name: Crayfish fly
baits.description: A fly that imitates a crayfish (a small freshwater lobster-like animal) crawling along the bottom.
baits.why: Smallmouth eat a lot of crayfish, so a crayfish fly pulled slowly along the bottom looks like one crawling over the rocks. Fly anglers call fly fishing a top way to catch smallmouth.
baits.hook: Tie the size 6 fly to the end of your leader; it comes with its own hook, so add no bait.

baits.name: Streamer

gear.name: Common carp
gear.where: In shallow water.

methods.name: Bottom
methods.summary: Let corn or dough bait sit on the bottom and wait for a bite.
steps: Tie the hook to the end of your line.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast it out and let it sink to the bottom.
Rest the rod and watch the line. Carp can take a while.
methods.bite: When the line pulls tight or the rod bends, lift the rod and hold on. Carp run hard, so let line slip off the reel.

methods.name: Fly
methods.summary: Cast a small fly to a carp you can see in shallow water.
steps: Look for carp in shallow water.
Tie the fly to the end of your line.
Cast the fly near a carp you can see.
Let it sink.
methods.bite: If you feel a pull or the line stops, lift the rod and pull the line tight.

baits.name: Corn
baits.description: Canned sweet corn, a pantry bait you put on the hook one or two kernels at a time.
baits.why: Corn isn't wild carp food, but carp feed mostly from the bottom and find food more by taste than sight, so sweet corn draws them. AZGFD recommends corn on a slip sinker rig in Phoenix-area ponds and lakes in the warm months.
baits.hook: Thread two or three kernels of canned corn onto the size 6 hook, covering the point.

baits.name: Dough bait
baits.description: A soft, sweet-smelling paste of flour or bread that you mold onto the hook.
baits.why: Carp feed on the bottom and find food more by taste than sight, so a sweet, flavored dough ball fished there draws them. Dough balls are one of the most common carp baits; wait, because carp can take a while.
baits.hook: Mold a marble-size ball of dough bait around the size 6 hook so the hook is covered.

baits.name: Nymph
baits.description: A small sinking fly that looks like an insect larva.
baits.why: Carp eat aquatic insects and other food off the bottom, so a nymph or crayfish fly looks like a meal. AZGFD says to cast 5–10 feet ahead of a carp you can see; carp craws worked in muddy water.
baits.hook: Tie the size 8 crayfish or carp nymph to the end of your line, cast 5–10 feet ahead of a carp you can see, and let it sink.

gear.name: Crappie
gear.where: Around brush and docks.

methods.name: Float
methods.summary: Hang a small jig under a float and wait for the float to dip.
bring: Small float (a bobber that clips onto the line)
steps: Go in early spring or fall, when they bite best.
Tie the jig to the end of your line.
Clip the float onto the line above the jig, so the jig hangs at least a foot off the bottom.
Cast near brush or a dock.
methods.bite: When the float goes under, lift the rod gently and reel in. Do not yank: crappie have soft mouths.

methods.name: Slip float
methods.summary: Hang a jig under a float that slides, so you can set how deep the jig hangs.
bring: Float stopper (a small knot or bead on your line that stops the float at the depth you pick)
Slip float (a bobber with a hole through it that slides along the line)
steps: Put the float stopper on your line, a few feet from the end.
Slide the slip float onto your line below the stopper.
Tie the jig to the end of your line.
Slide the stopper up or down to set how deep the jig hangs, at least a foot off the bottom. If you get no bites, try another depth.
Cast near brush or a dock. The jig sinks until the stopper reaches the float.
methods.bite: When the float goes under, lift the rod gently and reel in. Do not yank: crappie have soft mouths.

methods.name: Fly
methods.summary: Cast a fly that looks like a small fish or creature and pull it back by hand.
steps: Tie the streamer to the end of your line.
Cast it near brush or a dock.
Pull it back in short pulls.
methods.bite: If you feel a pull or the line stops, lift the rod and pull the line tight.

baits.name: Marabou jig
baits.description: A small weighted hook with a soft feather tail that flutters like a minnow or bug.
baits.why: Crappie eat minnows, young shad and insects, so a feathery 1/32 oz jig that flutters like one works. A float keeps it at one depth in front of brush, where crappie hold and bite slowly.
baits.hook: Tie the 1/32 oz marabou jig straight to your line, add no bait, and clip the float above it so the jig hangs at least a foot off the bottom.

baits.name: Tube jig
baits.description: A weighted hook with a hollow soft plastic body (the tube) that flutters as it sinks.
baits.why: Crappie eat small shad and bugs, so a hollow tube body fluttering on the fall looks like one. ODWC lists naturally colored tubes among the best crappie lures.
baits.hook: Tie the 1/32 oz tube jig straight to your line with the tube already on the weighted head and the hook point out, and set the float above it.

baits.name: Curly-tail grub
baits.description: A soft plastic body with a curling tail that wiggles as it sinks, threaded onto a small jig head.
baits.why: Crappie eat small shad, minnows and bugs, so a curly-tail grub wiggling as it sinks looks like one. AZGFD reports crappie biting 2-inch grubs bounced off the bottom, and Oklahoma lists curly-tail grubs.

baits.name: Streamer
baits.description: A fly that imitates a minnow or other small fish, from a small marabou one to a big sculpin pattern, pulled back in short strips.
baits.why: Minnows and young shad are what black crappie eat most, so a marabou streamer that pulses like a small minnow looks like a meal. Pull it back in short pulls along brush or weeds.
baits.hook: Tie the size 10 marabou streamer to the end of your leader; it comes already tied on its own hook.

methods.summary: Put a big bunch of nightcrawlers on a large hook and let it rest on the bottom.
bring: 2/0–6/0 circle hook (a round hook that sets itself)
1–4 oz sliding sinker (a weight with a hole; your line slides through it)
Swivel (a small metal link that stops the sinker)
12–20 in leader of 25–30 lb line (a short piece of line)
steps: Go at night, or at dusk.
Slide the sinker onto your line, then tie the swivel to the end.
Tie the hook to the leader, then tie the other end of the leader to the swivel.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast near sunken trees or a deep hole and let it settle on the bottom.
methods.bite: When the rod tip bends down and stays down, pick up the rod and reel in steadily. Do not jerk the rod: the circle hook sets itself.

baits.name: Cut bait
baits.description: A chunk of fresh fish (shad, carp or bluegill) cut to fit the hook.

baits.hook: Push the 2/0–6/0 circle hook once through a big chunk of fresh fish, not stink bait, through the skin, with the point out.

baits.name: Nightcrawler
baits.description: A big earthworm from a bait shop; you use a piece or the whole worm.
baits.why: Flatheads feed at night in deep holes and heavy cover, so a big squirming bunch of worms gives off scent and motion they can find in the dark. Minnesota DNR says flatheads take gobs of crawlers, mostly at dusk and night.

gear.name: Largemouth bass
gear.where: Near reeds and docks.

methods.name: Plastic worm
methods.summary: Cast a soft plastic worm with no weight and let it sink slowly.
bring: Size 3/0 worm hook (a wide hook made for soft plastic worms)
steps: Tie the hook to the end of your line.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast it near reeds or docks.
Let it sink slowly on a loose line.
methods.bite: If the line twitches or moves off, lift the rod hard and reel in.

methods.name: Crankbait
methods.summary: Cast a hard plastic lure with a lip that makes it dive and wobble as you reel it back.
steps: Go at first light.
Tie the crankbait to the end of your line.
Cast it along rocks.
Reel it back.
methods.bite: If you feel a tug, lift the rod and keep reeling.

methods.name: Fly
methods.summary: Cast a floating bug and make it pop on the surface.
steps: Go at dawn.
Tie the popper to the end of your line.
Cast it near reeds or docks.
Pull the line in short tugs so it pops on the surface.
methods.bite: If a fish takes the fly, lift the rod.

baits.name: Senko
baits.description: A thick, soft plastic stick worm that wiggles as it sinks.
baits.why: Bass eat fish, crayfish and big insects, so a 5 in green-pumpkin Senko's slow, wiggling fall looks like an easy meal, especially on slow days or in shallow cover. AZGFD reports name Senkos at Lake Pleasant, Roosevelt and the Lower Salt.
baits.hook: Push the 3/0 worm hook through the tip of the Senko's head, bring it out, turn it, and tuck the hook point back into the worm so it won't snag weeds.

baits.name: Squarebill crankbait
baits.description: A hard plastic lure with a flat lip that makes it dive and wobble as you reel it in.
baits.why: Small fish and crayfish are a bass's main foods, so a lipped crankbait that wobbles and bumps along looks like one. AZGFD reports a good crankbait bite early in the day, and suggests it when topwater slows.
baits.hook: Tie the squarebill straight to your 12–15 lb line; it has its own hooks, so add no bait.

baits.name: Popper
baits.description: A floating fly with a flat or rounded head that pops and splashes on the water like a frog or bug that fell in.
baits.why: Bass eat frogs, mice and bugs that fall in the water, so a popper's pop and splash looks like one; shallow bass come up for it at dawn and dusk. AZGFD says the post-spawn topwater bite is hot early and late.
baits.hook: Tie the popper to the end of your leader; it comes already tied on its own hook.

gear.name: Smallmouth bass
gear.where: Along rocks, and on rocky ledges and rock that sticks out into the water.

methods.name: Jig
methods.summary: Cast a soft lure on a small weighted hook and work it along the rocks.
bring: 1/8 oz jig head (a hook with a weighted head)
steps: Tie the jig head to the end of your line.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast it near rocks.
Reel it back along the rocks.
methods.bite: If the line twitches or moves off, lift the rod and reel in.

methods.name: Drop shot
methods.summary: Tie a hook about a foot above a weight, so a soft bait hangs just off the bottom.
bring: Size 1 drop-shot hook (a small hook made for this rig)
1/4 oz drop-shot weight (a small teardrop weight that ties to the end of your line)
steps: Tie the hook to your line, leaving about a foot of line hanging below the knot.
Tie the weight to the end of that hanging line.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast to a rocky ledge or rocky shore, let the weight sit on the bottom, and gently shake the rod tip.
methods.bite: Watch your line, because bites can be very light. If it twitches or moves off, lift the rod and reel in.

methods.name: Fly
methods.summary: Cast a fly that looks like a small fish or creature and pull it back by hand.
steps: Tie the fly to the end of your line.
Cast it near rocks.
Let it sink.
Pull it back slowly by hand.
methods.bite: If you feel a pull or the line stops, lift the rod and pull the line tight.

baits.name: Crayfish soft plastic
baits.description: A soft rubber lure shaped like a crayfish, made to bump along the bottom.
baits.why: Smallmouth eat a lot of crayfish, so a crayfish soft plastic bumped along the rocks looks like one. AZGFD reports say small soft plastic crayfish and jigs work in fall, and plastics on rocky shelves in spring.
baits.hook: Push the point of the 1/8 oz jig head into the nose of the plastic and out along its back, so the body hangs straight.

baits.name: Tube jig
baits.description: A weighted hook with a hollow soft plastic body (the tube) that flutters as it sinks.
baits.why: Smallmouth eat crayfish and small fish, so a tube's hollow, wiggling tentacles dropping through the water look like one. AZGFD reports tube jigs catching smallmouth at Lake Mohave and on rocky ledges at Lake Powell.
baits.hook: Slide the tube over the 1/8 oz jig head until the line-tie pokes out the closed end, with the hook point just outside the tube.

baits.name: Plastic worm
baits.description: A soft rubber worm, thick or thin, that you put on a hook and let sink slowly.
baits.why: Smallmouth eat fish, crayfish and large insects, so a thin worm hanging just off the bottom looks like an easy meal when they ignore bigger baits. AZGFD names small drop-shot worms and light, subtle plastics in summer.
baits.hook: Push the size 1 drop-shot hook through the worm's nose once, point out, so it hangs straight and quivers when you shake the rod.

baits.name: Swimbait
baits.description: A soft plastic minnow with a paddle tail that wiggles as you reel it in.
baits.why: Smallmouth eat small fish like shad, so a swimbait, a soft plastic minnow, looks like one. AZGFD reports say swimbaits keep producing smallmouth, including around rock ledges in 10–30 feet of water in June.
baits.hook: Push the size 1 drop-shot hook through the nose of the 3 in minnow plastic, point out, so it hangs level in the water.

baits.name: Crayfish fly
baits.description: A fly that imitates a crayfish (a small freshwater lobster-like animal) crawling along the bottom.
baits.why: Smallmouth eat a lot of crayfish, so a crayfish fly pulled slowly along the bottom looks like one crawling over the rocks. Fly anglers call fly fishing a top way to catch smallmouth.
baits.hook: Tie the size 6 fly to the end of your leader; it comes with its own hook, so add no bait.

baits.name: Streamer
baits.description: A fly that imitates a minnow or other small fish, from a small marabou one to a big sculpin pattern, pulled back in short strips.
baits.why: Smallmouth eat small fish and crayfish around rocks, so a sculpin (a small bottom fish) fly pulled slowly along the bottom looks like one. Oklahoma's wildlife agency lists sculpin-colored flies for smallmouth.
baits.hook: Tie the size 6 fly to the end of your leader; it comes with its own hook, so add no bait.

gear.name: Bluegill
gear.where: Near weeds, and around brush or logs in the water.

methods.name: Bobber
methods.summary: Hang bait under a bobber and wait for the bobber to dip.
steps: Tie the hook to the end of your line.
Clip the bobber onto the line 1 to 3 feet above the hook.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast near weeds.
methods.bite: When the bobber dips or goes under, lift the rod and reel in.

methods.name: Jig
methods.summary: Cast a tiny jig and reel it back slowly so it swims.
steps: Tie the jig to the end of your line.
Cast it past weeds, rocks or logs.
Reel it back slowly so it swims.
methods.bite: If the line twitches or moves off, lift the rod and reel in.

methods.name: Fly
methods.summary: Cast a light fly that floats on the water like an insect.
steps: Tie the foam spider to the end of your line.
Cast it near weeds.
Let it sit on the water.
methods.bite: If it disappears, lift the rod.

baits.name: Nightcrawler
baits.description: A big earthworm from a bait shop; you use a piece or the whole worm.
baits.why: Bluegill eat mostly insects and other small prey, and their small mouths limit what they can take, so a small piece of nightcrawler is the right size. AZGFD calls bluegill a good first fish; use a small bobber near the weeds where they hide.
baits.hook: Thread a piece of nightcrawler onto the size 10 hook, just enough to cover it.

baits.name: Tube jig
baits.description: A weighted hook with a hollow soft plastic body (the tube) that flutters as it sinks.
baits.why: Bluegill hunt by sight and go for small moving things like bugs and baby crayfish, so a tiny tube looks like one. AZGFD says to use 1/64–1/16 oz jigs; bluegill inspect before biting, so go slowly near weeds and rocks.
baits.hook: Tie the 1/64 oz tube jig straight to the end of your 4 lb line; the hook is part of the jig, so add no bait.

baits.name: Foam spider
baits.description: A small floating foam fly with rubber legs that looks like a bug on the water.
baits.why: Bluegill take small bugs from the surface, so a floating foam spider looks like one that fell in. AZGFD says they are shallow near vegetation in summer. Let it sit on the water.
baits.hook: Tie the size 10–12 foam spider to the end of your leader; it comes already tied on its own hook.

baits.name: Streamer

gear.name: Largemouth bass
gear.where: Near reeds and docks.

methods.name: Plastic worm
methods.summary: Cast a soft plastic worm with no weight and let it sink slowly.
bring: Size 3/0 worm hook (a wide hook made for soft plastic worms)
steps: Tie the hook to the end of your line.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast it near reeds or docks.
Let it sink slowly on a loose line.
methods.bite: If the line twitches or moves off, lift the rod hard and reel in.

methods.name: Crankbait
methods.summary: Cast a hard plastic lure with a lip that makes it dive and wobble as you reel it back.
steps: Go at first light.
Tie the crankbait to the end of your line.
Cast it along rocks.
Reel it back.
methods.bite: If you feel a tug, lift the rod and keep reeling.

methods.name: Fly
methods.summary: Cast a floating bug and make it pop on the surface.
steps: Go at dawn.
Tie the popper to the end of your line.
Cast it near reeds or docks.
Pull the line in short tugs so it pops on the surface.
methods.bite: If a fish takes the fly, lift the rod.

baits.name: Senko
baits.description: A thick, soft plastic stick worm that wiggles as it sinks.
baits.why: Bass eat fish, crayfish and big insects, so a 5 in green-pumpkin Senko's slow, wiggling fall looks like an easy meal, especially on slow days or in shallow cover. AZGFD reports name Senkos at Lake Pleasant, Roosevelt and the Lower Salt.
baits.hook: Push the 3/0 worm hook through the tip of the Senko's head, bring it out, turn it, and tuck the hook point back into the worm so it won't snag weeds.

baits.name: Squarebill crankbait
baits.description: A hard plastic lure with a flat lip that makes it dive and wobble as you reel it in.
baits.why: Small fish and crayfish are a bass's main foods, so a lipped crankbait that wobbles and bumps along looks like one. AZGFD reports a good crankbait bite early in the day, and suggests it when topwater slows.
baits.hook: Tie the squarebill straight to your 12–15 lb line; it has its own hooks, so add no bait.

baits.name: Popper
baits.description: A floating fly with a flat or rounded head that pops and splashes on the water like a frog or bug that fell in.
baits.why: Bass eat frogs, mice and bugs that fall in the water, so a popper's pop and splash looks like one; shallow bass come up for it at dawn and dusk. AZGFD says the post-spawn topwater bite is hot early and late.
baits.hook: Tie the popper to the end of your leader; it comes already tied on its own hook.

gear.name: Rainbow trout
gear.where: Near the shore when the water is cool, and in deeper water once it warms.

methods.name: Bottom
methods.summary: Let bait rest on the bottom with a sinker and wait for a bite.
bring: Sliding sinker (a weight with a hole for your line)
Small swivel (a metal link that stops the sinker)
18 in leader (a short piece of line)
steps: Slide the sinker onto your line, then tie on a small swivel (a metal link that stops the sinker).
Tie an 18 in leader (a short piece of line) to the other end of the swivel.
Tie the hook to the end of the leader.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast out and let the sinker settle on the bottom.
methods.bite: Trout bite lightly. When the line pulls or the rod tip bends, lift the rod with a gentle pull and reel in.

methods.name: Spinner
methods.summary: Cast a small lure with a spinning blade and reel it back.
steps: Tie the spinner to the end of your line.
Cast it out.
Reel it back slowly and steadily, and try a different speed on the next cast.
methods.bite: If you feel a tug, lift the rod and keep reeling.

methods.name: Fly
methods.summary: Cast a fly that looks like a small fish or creature and pull it back by hand.
steps: Tie the woolly bugger to the end of your line.
Cast it out.
Pull the line back in slowly by hand.
methods.bite: If you feel a pull or the line stops, lift the rod and pull the line tight.

baits.name: PowerBait
baits.description: Soft, scented, brightly colored dough you mold onto the hook; it is made to look and smell like the feed pellets hatchery trout grew up on.
baits.why: Hatchery trout grew up eating feed pellets, so scented, colored dough that smells and looks like a pellet works best in the first days after a stocking. AZGFD lists PowerBait among its top trout baits.
baits.hook: Press a small ball of PowerBait around the size 10–12 hook until no metal shows. Bring two or three colors, like rainbow or chartreuse.

baits.name: Nightcrawler
baits.description: A big earthworm from a bait shop; you use a piece or the whole worm.
baits.why: Trout pick worms and bugs off the bottom, so a nightcrawler piece resting there looks like food they know. AZGFD lists worms first among its best trout baits all year; they work well in cold water, when trout cruise the shore.
baits.hook: Thread a small piece of nightcrawler onto the size 10–12 hook, leaving a short tail to wiggle.

baits.name: Corn
baits.description: Canned sweet corn, a pantry bait you put on the hook one or two kernels at a time.
baits.why: Stocked rainbows grew up on feed pellets, so a bright, sweet-smelling kernel of corn on the bottom is easy to mistake for food. AZGFD names corn with worms and PowerBait as its best-bet trout baits.
baits.hook: Push one or two kernels of canned corn onto the size 10–12 hook so the point is covered.

baits.name: Inline spinner
baits.description: A small metal lure with a spinning blade that flashes and thumps as you reel it in.
baits.why: Trout eat small fish and bugs near shore in cool water, so a small spinner's flash and thump looks like one swimming off. AZGFD says to think small for trout, in silver, gold or copper.
baits.hook: Tie the 1/16–1/8 oz inline spinner, like a Panther Martin, straight to your line; it has its own hook, so add no bait.

baits.name: Woolly bugger
baits.description: A fuzzy fly with a long tail that looks like a leech or a small fish when pulled slowly.
baits.why: Trout eat leeches and small fish, so a woolly bugger pulled slowly near shore or along pool bottoms looks like one. AZGFD lists size 10 bead-headed Woolly Buggers as producing flies for stocked trout all winter.
baits.hook: Tie a size 10 woolly bugger to the end of your leader; it comes already tied on its own hook.

gear.name: Channel catfish
gear.where: On the bottom: in the deepest spots by day, and in shallower water after dark.

methods.name: Bottom
methods.summary: Let bait rest on the bottom with a sinker and wait for a bite.
bring: Size 2–4 circle hook (a round hook that sets itself)
1/2 oz sliding sinker (a weight with a hole; your line slides through it)
Swivel (a small metal link that stops the sinker)
12–18 in leader (a short piece of line)
steps: Slide the sinker onto your line, then tie the swivel to the end.
Tie the hook to the leader, then tie the other end of the leader to the swivel.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast out and let it settle on the bottom.
methods.bite: When the rod tip bends down and stays down, pick up the rod and reel in steadily. Do not jerk the rod: the circle hook sets itself.

methods.name: Cut bait
methods.summary: Put a chunk of fresh fish on the bottom where catfish feed at dusk.
bring: Size 2–4 circle hook (a round hook that sets itself)
1/2 oz sliding sinker (a weight with a hole; your line slides through it)
Swivel (a small metal link that stops the sinker)
12–18 in leader (a short piece of line)
steps: Go at dusk.
Slide the sinker onto your line, then tie the swivel to the end.
Tie the hook to the leader, then tie the other end of the leader to the swivel.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast off the deep side of a point (land sticking out into the water) and let it settle on the bottom.
methods.bite: When the rod tip bends down and stays down, pick up the rod and reel in steadily. Do not jerk the rod: the circle hook sets itself.

baits.name: Hot dog
baits.description: A plain hot dog cut into chunks, a cheap store-bought bait.
baits.why: Catfish hunt by smell, not sight, so the stronger a bait smells, the better: a cut hot dog leaks salty, fatty scent they follow along the bottom. Fish it deep in daytime and shallower after dark.
baits.hook: Cut the hot dog into bite-size chunks and thread one onto the size 2–4 circle hook, point out.

baits.name: Chicken liver
baits.description: Raw chicken liver from the grocery store, a soft and smelly bait.
baits.why: Catfish find food by smell, taste and touch, so raw liver that bleeds a strong scent of blood and meat along the bottom pulls them in from far off; the stronger and ranker, the better. Best at dusk and after dark.
baits.hook: Thread a piece of liver onto the size 2–4 circle hook two or three times so it stays on through the cast.

baits.name: Stink bait
baits.description: A smelly store-bought paste or dip bait sold in a tub.
baits.why: Catfish find food mostly by smell and taste, so the more rancid the better: stink bait is made to smell rotten, and the stench spreads far through the water. AZGFD reports name stink baits, dips and nuggets.
baits.hook: Press the store-bought stink bait onto a plastic worm or sponge on the size 2–4 hook so it does not wash off.

baits.name: Cut bait
baits.description: A chunk of fresh fish (shad, carp or bluegill) cut to fit the hook.
baits.why: Channel cats eat fish, insects and crayfish and feed at night, so a fresh chunk of shad, carp or bluegill on the bottom at dusk looks and smells like an easy meal. Use only those: other game fish can't be cut for bait in Arizona.
baits.hook: Cut a fresh fish into a chunk that covers the size 2–4 circle hook, and run the hook through the skin once with the point out.

gear.name: Crappie
gear.where: Around brush and docks.

methods.name: Float
methods.summary: Hang a small jig under a float and wait for the float to dip.
bring: Small float (a bobber that clips onto the line)
steps: Go in early spring or fall, when they bite best.
Tie the jig to the end of your line.
Clip the float onto the line above the jig, so the jig hangs at least a foot off the bottom.
Cast near brush or a dock.
methods.bite: When the float goes under, lift the rod gently and reel in. Do not yank: crappie have soft mouths.

methods.name: Slip float
methods.summary: Hang a jig under a float that slides, so you can set how deep the jig hangs.
bring: Float stopper (a small knot or bead on your line that stops the float at the depth you pick)
Slip float (a bobber with a hole through it that slides along the line)
steps: Put the float stopper on your line, a few feet from the end.
Slide the slip float onto your line below the stopper.
Tie the jig to the end of your line.
Slide the stopper up or down to set how deep the jig hangs, at least a foot off the bottom. If you get no bites, try another depth.
Cast near brush or a dock. The jig sinks until the stopper reaches the float.
methods.bite: When the float goes under, lift the rod gently and reel in. Do not yank: crappie have soft mouths.

methods.name: Fly
methods.summary: Cast a fly that looks like a small fish or creature and pull it back by hand.
steps: Tie the streamer to the end of your line.
Cast it near brush or a dock.
Pull it back in short pulls.
methods.bite: If you feel a pull or the line stops, lift the rod and pull the line tight.

baits.name: Marabou jig
baits.description: A small weighted hook with a soft feather tail that flutters like a minnow or bug.
baits.why: Crappie eat minnows, young shad and insects, so a feathery 1/32 oz jig that flutters like one works. A float keeps it at one depth in front of brush, where crappie hold and bite slowly.
baits.hook: Tie the 1/32 oz marabou jig straight to your line, add no bait, and clip the float above it so the jig hangs at least a foot off the bottom.

baits.name: Tube jig
baits.description: A weighted hook with a hollow soft plastic body (the tube) that flutters as it sinks.
baits.why: Crappie eat small shad and bugs, so a hollow tube body fluttering on the fall looks like one. ODWC lists naturally colored tubes among the best crappie lures.
baits.hook: Tie the 1/32 oz tube jig straight to your line with the tube already on the weighted head and the hook point out, and set the float above it.

baits.name: Curly-tail grub
baits.description: A soft plastic body with a curling tail that wiggles as it sinks, threaded onto a small jig head.
baits.why: Crappie eat small shad, minnows and bugs, so a curly-tail grub wiggling as it sinks looks like one. AZGFD reports crappie biting 2-inch grubs bounced off the bottom, and Oklahoma lists curly-tail grubs.
baits.hook: Tie the 1.5 in curly-tail jig straight to your line, tail already on the weighted head; the slip float sets how deep it hangs.

baits.hook: Tie the size 10 marabou streamer to the end of your leader; it comes already tied on its own hook.

gear.name: Walleye
gear.where: Along rocky shores, especially rock that sticks out into the water.

methods.name: Jig
methods.summary: Put a worm or leech on a weighted hook and drag it slowly along the bottom.
bring: 1/4–3/8 oz jig head (a hook with a weighted head)
steps: Fish in low light or at night.
Tie the jig head to the end of your line.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast it out.
Reel it back slowly, lifting and lowering the rod tip so the jig hops along the bottom.
methods.bite: If the line twitches, jumps or goes slack, lift the rod and reel in.

methods.name: Bottom bouncer
methods.summary: Drag a nightcrawler on a hook line behind a weight that bumps along the bottom, from a slowly moving boat.
bring: Bottom bouncer (a lead weight on a stiff wire arm that bumps along the bottom)
Crawler harness (a spinning blade and two hooks on a short line, made for nightcrawlers)
steps: Fish in low light or at night.
Tie the bottom bouncer to the end of your line.
Tie the crawler harness behind it, so it trails 2 to 3 feet back.
Put your bait on the hook.
Let the weight touch the bottom, then slowly drag it along a rocky shore.
methods.bite: If the line twitches or moves off, lift the rod and reel in.

methods.name: Fly
methods.summary: Cast a fly that looks like a small fish or creature and pull it back by hand.
steps: Fish in low light or at night.
Tie the Clouser to the end of your line.
Cast it out.
Let it sink.
Pull it back in short pulls.
methods.bite: If you feel a pull or the line stops, lift the rod and pull the line tight.

baits.name: Nightcrawler
baits.description: A big earthworm from a bait shop; you use a piece or the whole worm.
baits.why: Walleye eat fish, insects and crayfish, mostly in low light, so a crawler wriggling on the bottom looks like an easy meal. AZGFD says nightcrawlers are a good bet for walleye; Iowa DNR advises crawlers in summer.
baits.hook: On the jig, thread the crawler on the hook (half a crawler is fine); on the harness, front on one hook, back on the other.

baits.name: Leech
baits.description: A live leech (a soft, wriggly pond worm), sold at bait shops.
baits.why: Walleye eat fish, insects and crayfish, mostly in low light, so a leech wriggling off a jig looks like an easy meal on the bottom. Iowa DNR advises leeches or crawlers in late spring, summer and early fall.
baits.hook: Hook the leech once through the sucker disk (its flat end) so it wiggles on the jig head.

baits.name: Clouser minnow
baits.description: A fly with lead eyes that dips and rises like a small baitfish when you pull the line in short tugs.
baits.why: Walleye eat mostly fish and feed in low light, so a Clouser, a weighted fly pulled in short tugs, dips like a baitfish; in dark colors it can pass for a leech. Fish it at night or at dawn.
baits.hook: Tie the size 4 Clouser to your leader; it has its own hook, so add no bait.

gear.name: Yellow bass
gear.where: In schools, just off the bottom.

methods.name: Bobber
methods.summary: Hang bait under a bobber and wait for the bobber to dip.
steps: Tie the hook to the end of your line.
Clip the bobber onto the line so the bait hangs just above the bottom.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast it out.
methods.bite: When the bobber goes under, lift the rod and reel in.

methods.name: Jig
methods.summary: Cast a small weighted hook with a bit of worm and bounce it just off the bottom.
bring: 1/16 oz white or chartreuse jig (a hook with a weighted head)
steps: Tie the jig to the end of your line.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast near a school of fish.
Let it sink to the bottom.
Lift and drop it, keeping it within a few inches of the bottom.
methods.bite: If the line twitches or moves off, lift the rod and reel in.

methods.name: Fly
methods.summary: Cast a fly that looks like a small fish or creature and pull it back by hand.
steps: Tie the fly to the end of your line.
Cast it near a school of fish.
Pull it back in short pulls.
methods.bite: If you feel a pull or the line stops, lift the rod and pull the line tight.

baits.name: Nightcrawler
baits.description: A big earthworm from a bait shop; you use a piece or the whole worm.
baits.why: Yellow bass feed heavily on small creatures on the bottom, so a small piece of nightcrawler is real food. AZGFD names small nightcrawler pieces for yellow bass; Iowa DNR says a piece about an inch long is plenty.
baits.hook: Thread a 1 in piece of nightcrawler onto the size 8 hook (or the jig) so it covers the point.

baits.name: Streamer
baits.description: A fly that imitates a minnow or other small fish, from a small marabou one to a big sculpin pattern, pulled back in short strips.
baits.why: Yellow bass eat small fish and bottom insects, so a small white streamer pulled in short tugs and kept low looks like a minnow on the move.
baits.hook: Tie the size 8 streamer to your leader; it has its own hook, so add no bait.

baits.name: Clouser minnow
baits.description: A fly with lead eyes that dips and rises like a small baitfish when you pull the line in short tugs.
baits.why: Adult yellow bass eat fish and school near the surface, so a Clouser, a weighted fly pulled in short tugs, dips like a small baitfish. It is a proven fly for white bass, a close relative.
baits.hook: Tie the size 8 Clouser to your leader; it has its own hook, so add no bait.

baits.hook: Tie the 1/64 oz tube jig straight to the end of your 4 lb line; the hook is part of the jig, so add no bait.

baits.name: Foam spider
baits.description: A small floating foam fly with rubber legs that looks like a bug on the water.
baits.why: Bluegill take small bugs from the surface, so a floating foam spider looks like one that fell in. AZGFD says they are shallow near vegetation in summer. Let it sit on the water.
baits.hook: Tie the size 10–12 foam spider to the end of your leader; it comes already tied on its own hook.

gear.name: Rainbow trout
gear.where: Near the shore when the water is cool, and in deeper water once it warms.

methods.name: Bottom
methods.summary: Let bait rest on the bottom with a sinker and wait for a bite.
bring: Sliding sinker (a weight with a hole for your line)
Small swivel (a metal link that stops the sinker)
18 in leader (a short piece of line)
steps: Slide the sinker onto your line, then tie on a small swivel (a metal link that stops the sinker).
Tie an 18 in leader (a short piece of line) to the other end of the swivel.
Tie the hook to the end of the leader.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast out and let the sinker settle on the bottom.
methods.bite: Trout bite lightly. When the line pulls or the rod tip bends, lift the rod with a gentle pull and reel in.

methods.name: Spinner
methods.summary: Cast a small lure with a spinning blade and reel it back.
steps: Tie the spinner to the end of your line.
Cast it out.
Reel it back slowly and steadily, and try a different speed on the next cast.
methods.bite: If you feel a tug, lift the rod and keep reeling.

methods.name: Fly
methods.summary: Cast a fly that looks like a small fish or creature and pull it back by hand.
steps: Tie the woolly bugger to the end of your line.
Cast it out.
Pull the line back in slowly by hand.
methods.bite: If you feel a pull or the line stops, lift the rod and pull the line tight.

baits.name: PowerBait
baits.description: Soft, scented, brightly colored dough you mold onto the hook; it is made to look and smell like the feed pellets hatchery trout grew up on.

baits.name: Nightcrawler
baits.description: A big earthworm from a bait shop; you use a piece or the whole worm.

baits.name: Corn
baits.description: Canned sweet corn, a pantry bait you put on the hook one or two kernels at a time.

baits.name: Inline spinner
baits.description: A small metal lure with a spinning blade that flashes and thumps as you reel it in.

gear.name: Largemouth bass
gear.where: Near reeds and docks.

Put your bait on the hook.
Cast it near reeds or docks.
Let it sink slowly on a loose line.

Reel it back.

Tie the popper to the end of your line.

baits.why: Flatheads feed at night in deep holes and heavy cover, so a big squirming bunch of worms gives off scent and motion they can find in the dark. Minnesota DNR says flatheads take gobs of crawlers, mostly at dusk and night.
baits.hook: Thread a big bunch of nightcrawlers onto the 2/0–6/0 circle hook until the hook is buried in a squirming ball.

gear.name: Largemouth bass
gear.where: Near reeds and docks.

methods.name: Plastic worm
methods.summary: Cast a soft plastic worm with no weight and let it sink slowly.
bring: Size 3/0 worm hook (a wide hook made for soft plastic worms)
steps: Tie the hook to the end of your line.
Put your bait on the hook.
Cast it near reeds or docks.
Let it sink slowly on a loose line.
methods.bite: If the line twitches or moves off, lift the rod hard and reel in.

methods.name: Crankbait
methods.summary: Cast a hard plastic lure with a lip that makes it dive and wobble as you reel it back.
steps: Go at first light.
Tie the crankbait to the end of your line.
Cast it along rocks.
Reel it back.
methods.bite: If you feel a tug, lift the rod and keep reeling.

methods.name: Fly
methods.summary: Cast a floating bug and make it pop on the surface.
steps: Go at dawn.
Tie the popper to the end of your line.
Cast it near reeds or docks.
Pull the line in short tugs so it pops on the surface.
methods.bite: If a fish takes the fly, lift the rod.

baits.name: Senko
baits.description: A thick, soft plastic stick worm that wiggles as it sinks.
baits.why: Bass eat fish, crayfish and big insects, so a 5 in green-pumpkin Senko's slow, wiggling fall looks like an easy meal, especially on slow days or in shallow cover. AZGFD reports name Senkos at Lake Pleasant, Roosevelt and the Lower Salt.
baits.hook: Push the 3/0 worm hook through the tip of the Senko's head, bring it out, turn it, and tuck the hook point back into the worm so it won't snag weeds.

baits.name: Squarebill crankbait
baits.description: A hard plastic lure with a flat lip that makes it dive and wobble as you reel it in.
baits.why: Small fish and crayfish are a bass's main foods, so a lipped crankbait that wobbles and bumps along looks like one. AZGFD reports a good crankbait bite early in the day, and suggests it when topwater slows.
baits.hook: Tie the squarebill straight to your 12–15 lb line; it has its own hooks, so add no bait.

baits.name: Popper
baits.description: A floating fly with a flat or rounded head that pops and splashes on the water like a frog or bug that fell in.
baits.why: Bass eat frogs, mice and bugs that fall in the water, so a popper's pop and splash looks like one; shallow bass come up for it at dawn and dusk. AZGFD says the post-spawn topwater bite is hot early and late.
baits.hook: Tie the popper to the end of your leader; it comes already tied on its own hook.
